title: O death, where is your sting? (1 Corinthians 15:55)

cards: For most of a long chapter, Paul has been arguing in careful steps: if this, then that, seeds and stars and the order of things. Then, near the end, the argument breaks open.
He turns, the way someone turns on a bully who has finally lost his grip, and speaks straight to death. Not about death. To it.
He calls it by name, the way you'd call across a schoolyard, and asks it a mocking question. It's short, and it's fierce.

teach.b: Here are the lines: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" First, they're borrowed.
Paul echoes the prophet Hosea, where the King James has God say: "O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction."
Readers of Hosea argue over whether that line is a promise or a threat in its own chapter. In Paul's hands, it's a taunt. Second, the sting.
Paul's Greek word can mean an insect's stinger, or the sharp goad a farmer used to drive an ox: the point that does the damage.

teach.h: THE STING IS THE POINT THAT HURTS.
teach.b: And Paul names that point: "The sting of death is sin." Some readers hear in that line that the hurt of death isn't only the ending; it's everything left broken, unforgiven, undone.
Third, thanks: "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul isn't pretending people have stopped dying.
He claims death has already lost, because of the resurrection the whole chapter is about. Its point has been pulled.
Fourth, the taunt ends in work. The very next verse: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord."

Not a shout and then a nap; a shout, and then back to the job. Long after, the poet John Donne caught the same nerve in a sonnet that tells Death not to be proud, and ends by saying that death itself shall die.

how: 1 Corinthians 15 is read in the burial service of the Book of Common Prayer, and its taunt to death is sung in Handel's Messiah.

o: a mourner's cry of grief at a graveside
a prayer asking death to come quickly
the start of Paul's taunt: where is thy sting?

p: O death, I will be thy plagues

s: Paul made up the taunt to death himself
he's echoing the prophet Hosea: "O death, I will be thy plagues."
Paul says people have stopped dying
he says death has already lost, through Christ's resurrection. its sting has been pulled.
right after the taunt, Paul tells his readers to keep working
"be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord."

games.q: you're Paul. you've just taunted death: where is thy sting? what do you tell your readers next?
o: relax; nothing you do matters now.
be steadfast, keep working; your labor is not in vain.
go and look for death to prove you're not afraid.
games.why: "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord." the taunt doesn't end in rest. it sends people back to work.

practice: Let one fear come up, about death or something smaller that feels like a little death, losing a job, a friend, getting older, and look at it squarely.
If you pray, say Paul's line to it quietly, where is thy sting; if you don't, ask the fear a question back instead of only listening to it. Notice whether it shrinks, even a little.

wordCard.voice: O death. The opening of Paul's taunt in First Corinthians fifteen, borrowed from Hosea: O death, where is thy sting?

orig.note: Greek: where, O death, is your sting? kentron is a stinger, or a farmer's goad.

carryVoice: Your line: where is your sting? Death's point has been pulled. Back tomorrow, same hill.
